introduction: I enjoy exploring how simple mechanics can come together to create varied gameplay experiences. My projects span combat, systems, and level design, with a focus on developing ideas into playable experiences.

selectedWork.title: Skill Inheritance Action Combat Prototype

selectedWork.title: Soft Things Hit Hard

prototypes.title: Anchor Boat
overview: A demo built around a movement restriction: the boat cannot steer directly left or right. Players swing around anchors and release to launch. I wanted to explore whether restricting movement could create interesting choices. Holding an anchor keeps the boat swinging; releasing it launches the boat along its current direction, either horizontally or upward.
prototypes.description: A demo built around a movement restriction: the boat cannot steer directly left or right. Players swing around anchors and release to launch. I wanted to explore whether restricting movement could create interesting choices. Holding an anchor keeps the boat swinging; releasing it launches the boat along its current direction, either horizontally or upward.
prototypes.body:
Giving Movement a Purpose

Enemies advance toward a central objective. Players attack them through movement: swinging deals low collision damage and increases automatic turret fire rate. A horizontal launch can hit enemies along its path, while an upward launch deals area damage on landing. Players can choose their movement based on enemy positions.

prototypes.title: Tower Trade-off
overview: A tower-defense demo exploring what happens when players give up a familiar gameplay choice.

Players first choose both tower types and locations. After winning, they give up one choice and defend against the same waves on the same map: 1. Keep the choice of tower locations, but tower types are randomized. 2. Keep the choice of tower types, but locations are randomized.
prototypes.description: A tower-defense demo exploring what happens when players give up a familiar gameplay choice.
prototypes.body:
Findings & Reflection

In my playtesting, random placement was more punishing: short-range towers could land beyond reach of the path, making success heavily dependent on luck. Repeatedly choosing the longest-range tower had a clear advantage. Randomizing tower types while keeping placement control was easier. This showed that the two sacrifices were not equivalent. Placement could determine whether a tower contributed at all, making long range the safest response to uncertainty. Removing one choice can also narrow the remaining options. A meaningful sacrifice needs room for adaptation, rather than making options ineffective.

prototypes.title: Spatial Flip Puzzle
overview: This prototype challenged my spatial puzzle design skills. Players use buttons to flip individual cubes, rows, or columns by 180 degrees, rearranging the space to connect a route to the exit.
prototypes.description: This prototype challenged my spatial puzzle design skills. Players use buttons to flip individual cubes, rows, or columns by 180 degrees, rearranging the space to connect a route to the exit.
prototypes.body:
I began with a Rubik's Cube-inspired rotation mechanic, aiming for complex puzzles players could solve through step-by-step reasoning. Designing those levels proved difficult, and the final layout was largely linear.

Findings & Reflection

During playtesting, the number of buttons, available operations, and spatial changes left players disoriented. They began trying inputs at random rather than identifying patterns and working through a solution as intended. The level was solvable, but the experience exposed a gap between solvability and readability. Tracking the changing space interfered with the intended reasoning. Testing a spatial puzzle needs to examine whether players can understand what an action changed and use that understanding to plan their next move, alongside checking that a solution exists.

prototypes.title: God of Words
overview: A party game combining secret bidding with word building.
Core Design Keywords: Multilateral Competition · Auction · Alignment · Involving a Secret That Complicates Player Interactions
The design connects secret bids for letter-picking priority with assembling and presenting a themed answer.
prototypes.description: A party game combining secret bidding with word building.
prototypes.body: ## Gameplay: Bid, Build an Answer, and Persuade Players share a theme and receive a limited budget. Each auction reveals letters, and players secretly bid for picking priority. Everyone participating pays their own bid. Higher bids choose first. Players weigh securing a useful letter against saving money for later, and can skip unwanted auctions. Dedicated vowel auctions offer opportunities to complete an idea. The collected letters become the material for a themed answer. Players do not need to use every letter: words, phrases, abbreviations, and non-English answers are allowed if the group accepts their connection to the theme. Everyone reveals and explains their answer, then secretly votes for another player's response. The player with the most votes wins. This connects two forms of play: planning which letters to pursue and improvising an interpretation from the letters obtained. ## Iteration: More Choice Within the Constraint Early feedback showed that spending more did not reliably secure a desired letter. We changed the auction to ranked picking, replaced later random vowel draws with vowel auctions, and allowed players to skip rather than pay for unwanted letters. The supply of letters remained limited, and we did not add trading at the end of the game. This preserved the trade-offs in bidding. ## Adjusting the Auction Phase The ending shifted from players exhausting their budgets to a round limit. Initially, the round limit matched the number of players, but four rounds felt too short in a four-player game, so we increased it. However, six-player tests with nine rounds outlasted some players' interest once they had an answer ready. We settled on six rounds before the reveal and voting.

prototypes.title: Sprawl
overview: A territory-control game where players grow vines across a shared board, competing for space while keeping their own growth routes alive.
Core Design Keywords: Multilateral Competition · Territory Control · Construction · Involving Nature
Vine growth connects construction and territory control: players build branching paths and cut off their opponents' growth.
prototypes.description: A territory-control game where players grow vines across a shared board, competing for space while keeping their own growth routes alive.
prototypes.body: ## Gameplay: Expand, Cut Off, and Survive Action cards determine the size of vine tile players may place. Players choose a shape and orientation, then connect it to an open growing tip of their vine. Placement can extend a route, create branches, or cover opponents' vines. Growing tips are both expansion points and vulnerable targets. Covering an opponent's tip removes that growth option and earns bonus points. Losing every tip eliminates a player. Visible territory scores at the end, while the last surviving vine wins immediately. Players therefore weigh expanding their area against cutting off rivals and preserving their own tips. In addition, item cards can protect a board space or grant an additional action on the next turn. ## Iteration: Creating Conflict and Preserving Planning Early tests allowed too much independent expansion. We reduced the initial 13×13 board to 9×9, introduced elimination through blocked tips, and rewarded covering opponents' tips to encourage direct competition. Initially, players drew a random shape after an action card determined its size. This could invalidate a planned move. Allowing shape selection removed that second layer of randomness while retaining the action-card constraint. ## Reflection We were satisfied with the territory-control experience at around 40–60 minutes, but the assignment required under 20. Further board reductions to 7×7, fewer rounds, and additional opening placements aimed to compress the experience. However, a later report still recorded a 45-minute session. This experience showed me that play time depends on more than board size and round count. The metagame takes time: players think through moves, talk, and try to read one another. Keeping these interactions while fitting a session into 20 minutes was a challenge for us. Players enjoyed attacking one another and trying to anticipate each other's next move. However, overlapping vines made it hard to see which sections were connected and which tips could still grow. We revised the rule wording, diagrams, and indicators to help players read the board more easily.

prototypes.title: Tapper Recreation
overview: A Unity recreation of Tapper's multi-lane serving loop. Players switch counters, serve drinks to push customers back, and catch returning mugs while managing pressure across lanes.
prototypes.description: A Unity recreation of Tapper's multi-lane serving loop. Players switch counters, serve drinks to push customers back, and catch returning mugs while managing pressure across lanes.
prototypes.body: I handled the primary gameplay implementation through observation of the original game and AI-assisted development. Level configurations use ScriptableObjects to define per-lane customer queues, repeat counts, queue spacing, and respawn delays, keeping these settings separate from the shared gameplay code.

analyses.title: The “Overloaded Hero” Problem in Honor of Kings - A Case Study of Chicha
paragraphs: When does a versatile hero offer meaningful choices, and when does it leave too few weaknesses or counterplay options? Using Chicha's weapon rotation as a case study, I examine the trade-offs behind functional coverage, form progression, and lane flexibility, then propose clearer roles and limits for each form.

analyses.title: Why The Bazaar Is Fun - and Keeps Me Coming Back
paragraphs: What makes The Bazaar fun, and why is it so easy to keep playing? I explore the satisfaction of discovering item combinations and watching them work, and how each fight gives players something else to try. A Vanessa build illustrates how item pools, board space, and tags turn individual effects into combinations worth pursuing.

about: Hi, I'm Ethan. I study Game Development and Interactive Design at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles.

I play a wide range of games, especially strategy, roguelite, puzzle, and competitive multiplayer titles. I enjoy figuring out how their mechanics work together and exploring the different choices they give players.

I'm especially interested in how a few simple mechanics can create different ways to play. In my own designs, I want to give players room to experiment, discover combinations, and develop their own approaches.

Outside of game development, I make videos and music. I've posted videos about music, daily life, and games on Bilibili. I enjoy exploring different musical styles, from electronic tracks to instrumental compositions. You can listen to some of my music on the Audio page.

I'd describe myself as thoughtful and patient. I like hearing how other people see a problem, and I'm comfortable reconsidering an idea when a conversation or playtest gives me a reason to. I enjoy working with people who bring different perspectives.

overdawn.title: Overdawn
paragraphs: Overdawn is a 2.5D dystopian shooter. Demo released on Steam. I led its three-person audio team and personally created over 100 sound assets for combat, abilities, UI, and environments.
